glosses.text: nifkadta, “you will be missed”; the same root as yippaked, “remains vacant,” and again in vv. 25 and 27. The empty seat is the plot.
Ezel: a place-name, or “the stone of going,” a wayside marker. Septuagint: “that mound.” Compare v. 41.
mikreh, “a chance happening”: the Torah’s euphemism for a nocturnal emission (Deut. 23:11).
na‘avat, “perverse, twisted”: a rare form. The insult reaches Jonathan through his mother, Ahinoam (14:50).
higdil, literally “made great,” hence “wept the longer.” Septuagint: “until a great finish.” Often emended.

commentary.lemma: Tomorrow will be the new moon
commentary.text: When the New Moon occurs on Shabbat, they read as the haftarah “And it shall come to pass that every New Moon” (Isaiah 66). When it occurs on Sunday, on the previous day they read as the haftarah “And Jonathan said to him: Tomorrow is the New Moon.”

You will be remembered: my father will recall you when your seat stands empty of the one who sits in it. Yippaked means lacking, as in “not one of us is missing” (Numbers 31:49). Targum Jonathan: “you will be sought, for the place where you recline will be empty.”

commentary.lemma: Tomorrow will be the new moon
commentary.text: Jonathan answers both things David may have meant by “who will tell me?” (v. 10). If David meant “will you tell me the truth,” Jonathan swears by the God of Israel that he will sound out his father. If he meant “how will you tell me without anyone noticing,” Jonathan answers: tomorrow is the new moon, everyone who eats at the king’s table comes on the festival, and your empty seat will speak for you.
A stone that was a landmark for travelers; ha-ozel, “those who go.” So Targum Jonathan renders it even ata, “the stone that served as a sign.”

All three days, today, tomorrow, and the day after, go well down into the valley and stay hidden where you hid “on the day of the deed,” the day Saul swore to Jonathan that he would not kill you (19:6), for you were hidden in that place then too.

commentary.lemma: the promise we made to each other
commentary.text: The oath of vv. 12–17 and 42 is the legal spine of the David story. It explains why David later spares and feeds Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9) and gives him grounds to execute other Saulides (2 Samuel 21) without breaking faith. For a narrator defending David against the charge of usurpation, a covenant freely offered by the heir is the strongest possible evidence.
commentary.cites: P. Kyle McCarter Jr., I Samuel, Anchor Bible (1980); Robert Alter, The David Story (1999)

commentary.text: Due to a nocturnal emission or some other reason; surely he did not come to eat from the sacred offering as he has not yet ritually purified himself. This common form of impurity would be the most obvious explanation for an unexpected absence. Saul assumed David would come the next day, after immersing, in accordance with Deuteronomy 23:11–12.

Saul’s first explanation is cultic, not political. The meal is a zevach, a sacrificial feast (v. 29), and whoever eats of it must be pure (Leviticus 7:20–21). This scene is the Bible’s fullest glimpse of the pre-exilic new-moon festival as a court occasion, with a fixed seating order and a two-day observance (vv. 27, 34) that may reflect uncertainty about when the month began.
commentary.cites: McCarter, I Samuel; The Jewish Study Bible, 2nd ed. (2014)

commentary.lemma: son of a perverse, rebellious woman
commentary.text: Na‘avat is from na, to stray and wander: a gadding woman. Another explanation: when the Benjaminites seized the girls of Shiloh who came out to dance in the vineyards (Judges 21), Saul was bashful and would not seize one, until she herself came, behaving brazenly, and pursued him.

commentary.lemma: son of a perverse, rebellious woman
commentary.text: “You son of a perverse and strongly rebellious woman! Do I not know that you love the son of Jesse to your own shame and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?”

The phrase names rebellion in the abstract. A servant may rebel against his master to throw off the yoke or to reign in his place; a son does not rebel against his father in order to enthrone a stranger. If it happens, it is a rebellion of madness and twisted reason. “I know you have chosen the son of Jesse” for this very end; remember that it is “to your shame and the shame of your mother’s nakedness,” for the kingship will pass from her line to a stranger.
Saul cursed and shamed Yehonatan’s mother. He further sharpened his outburst, employing coarse, disrespectful language: you prefer that David shall become king, to your own shame.

commentary.lemma: neither you nor your kingship will be secure
commentary.text: The insult reaches Jonathan through his mother, a pattern of abuse attested across the ancient Near East; “your mother’s nakedness” borrows the vocabulary of the incest laws (Leviticus 18:7–8), as if Jonathan’s loyalty exposed the royal house itself. Then Saul says aloud what the narrator has been arguing since chapter 16: as long as David lives, Jonathan will never reign. Critics read vv. 30–31 as the thesis of the History of David’s Rise, placed in the mouth of its chief opponent.

Until David exceeded: he wept more. Ralbag reads it as “more than was fitting.” David wept more than Jonathan because Jonathan could go home, while David now had to flee from Saul, who sought his life.

commentary.lemma: They kissed each other and wept together
commentary.text: They knew they would probably not meet again. Yehonatan loved David no less than David loved Yehonatan; but David knew that from then on he was doomed to a life of hardship, persecution, and suffering.

The Hebrew is in trouble here. “The Negeb” (the southern desert) makes no sense in a field outside Gibeah and is almost certainly a corruption of the “Ezel” of v. 19, as the JPS note allows. “David wept the longer” translates a phrase the Greek read differently. Samuel is the Hebrew Bible’s most damaged book textually, and 4QSamᵃ from Qumran often sides with the Greek against the received text.
commentary.cites: McCarter, I Samuel; Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (2012)

commentary.text: The haftarah closes on the oath rather than on the parting, so that what the congregation hears last is the covenant “between your offspring and mine, forever.” Chapter 21 opens with David on the road.

glossary.text: Saul’s cousin and the commander of his army (14:50). He sits at the king’s side at the feast and later becomes a power broker between the houses of Saul and David.
David’s hometown in Judah, a few miles south of Jerusalem. The “family feast” there is David’s alibi, or Jonathan’s invention.
A landmark stone in the open country outside Gibeah, the agreed hiding place. See the margin note at v. 19.
Saul’s capital, in Benjamin just north of Jerusalem; the unnamed “town” of vv. 40–41.
David’s father. Saul never says David’s name in this chapter, only “the son of Jesse,” a slight that the narrator lets us hear.
Saul’s eldest son and heir, a war hero (chapters 13–14), bound to David by covenant since 18:3.
Rosh Chodesh, the first day of the lunar month, marked by sacrifices (Numbers 28:11–15) and here by a two-day royal feast.
“The south,” the desert region of Judah. In v. 41 the word is probably a scribal error for Ezel.

openingNote.calendar: Read in place of the usual haftarah for Bereshit, Isaiah 42:5–43:10. When Rosh Chodesh falls on a Sunday, the Shabbat before it takes this reading (Megillah 31a): its first words announce a new moon tomorrow. This Shabbat is 29 Tishrei, the eve of Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan.
setting: Samuel belongs to the Former Prophets, a history most scholars read as a Deuteronomistic work of the late seventh and sixth centuries BCE, built from older sources. One of them, the History of David’s Rise (1 Samuel 16 to 2 Samuel 5), argues scene by scene that David did not seize Saul’s throne but was given it, and that Saul’s own son recognized him first. Our chapter is the hinge of that argument: Jonathan, the heir, binds himself to David by covenant and is cursed by his father for it.

The setting is the new-moon feast, a court festival older than the written Torah’s calendar, with a fixed seating order and a requirement of ritual purity. The Hebrew of Samuel is the most damaged in the Bible; the Greek and the Qumran scroll preserve readings the Masoretic Text has lost, and the margin notes flag where this week’s verses are read differently.
